newsitem.title: USA: CEO turning Ben & Jerry's over to marketing specialist.
newsitem.headline: CEO turning Ben & Jerry's over to marketing specialist.

text.p: Robert Holland said Friday that he was resigning as president and chief executive of Ben & Jerry's Homemade Inc. to allow a marketing specialist to take the helm of the ice cream maker as it seeks to expand overseas.

"The reasons I'm making way for a new CEO is that I have good instincts, but not world-class experience in the consumer goods business," Holland said in a telephone interview after announcing he was leaving the Vermont-based company known for its quirky product names and corporate largesse.

Holland and company co-founder Ben Cohen both said the 56-year-old Holland's departure, on Oct. 31, will come at a time when many of the goals he faced upon taking over less than two years ago have been met.
Still, the company's stock lost $1, or almost 8 percent, after the news was announced. The shares later recovered a bit to trade at $12.75, down 50 cents, in afternoon trading on Nasdaq.

Ben & Jerry's said this month it expected third-quarter earnings to be "materially" below last year's, but Holland said things were improving as the company battles archrival Haagen-Daz for sales in the market for premium ice cream, which is about 2 percent of all ice-cream sales.
"Our earnings are back on track to where they were before the third quarter," Holland said. "We're away from the precipice. Our earnings are solid."

Holland replaced the firm's famous founders early in 1995, when the company -- originally known for its counter-culture corporate culture -- moved from a "founder-led" system to a more professional management structure.

As health-conscious Americans began swearing off fattening foods, Holland was brought in to introduce the company's products, like "Cherry Garcia" and "Chunky Monkey" ice cream, to sweet-toothed consumers overseas.

The no-nonsense, button-downed executive -- the antithesis of the bearded, tie-dyed founders of the company, whose scruffy visages appear on every pint -- did manage to restore order to Ben & Jerry's operations and finances.

Holland said the ice cream maker's expansion into Europe was on target, although "not as fast as I would like," and Ben & Jerry's would enter the Japanese market with an eye on the entire Pacific Rim.

However, with premium ice cream in countries like Britain selling at twice the price of lower-priced brands, Holland said, a highly experienced marketing executive with international skills was needed to run the company.
"We've got a pretty sophisticated challenge," he said from the company's new headquarters in Burlington, Vt.
He said a key challenge to boosting sales was to get more consumers to make a taste test. Many people who buy a first pint are repeat buyers, but that getting that first trial is difficult.

Holland, a former chief executive of a plastics firm and consultant to Fortune 500 companies, took over at Ben & Jerry's in February 1995 with great fanfare after Cohen stepped up to the role of chairman.
He was hired after the company launched an unorthodox search campaign through newspaper advertisements in which it invited candidates to write essays explaining why they were suited for the job.

After receiving more than 22,500 responses to its "Yo, I'm Your CEO" write-in campaign, Ben & Jerry's hired Holland, although there were reports that he was actually found through an executive search firm.

"Bob arrived just when we needed him to help straighten out our operations, get our new plant up and running, start our international business and launch our new sorbet line. We are very grateful for his contribution," said Cohen, who with Jerry Greenfield turned a correspondence course in ice cream-making into a $150 million company.

Holland said that in addition to its overseas expansion, the company had also upgraded its manufacturing operations and improved employee morale, once said to be on the decline, under a new human resources director.
"Ben & Jerry's has great products, great people and a promising future," Holland said in a statement.
The company, however, does not have a successor for Holland, who will remain as a director through June 1997.

Bruce Bowman, senior director of operations, was given the additional title of chief operating officer on an interim basis and will oversee day-to-day management of the company until a successor to Holland is found.
The company said a subcommittee of the board would begin a search for a new CEO immediately.
